# Likelihood as a weighted syndrome problem

Let $H\in\mathbb{F}_2^{m\times n}$ be a binary syndrome matrix, $e\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$ an error vector, and $s=He$ the measured syndrome. If the coordinates fail independently with probabilities $p_i<1/2$, then

$$
\Pr(e)=\prod_{i=1}^n p_i^{e_i}(1-p_i)^{1-e_i}.
$$

Discarding an additive constant from $-\log\Pr(e)$ gives the weight

$$
w_i=\log\frac{1-p_i}{p_i},
\qquad
W(e)=\sum_{i=1}^n w_ie_i.
$$

::: {#def-mwpm-error-ml .callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition: error maximum-likelihood decoding

The error-ML problem is

$$
\min_{e\in\mathbb{F}_2^n}
\sum_iw_ie_i
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
He=s.
$$
:::

For identical $p_i=p<1/2$, all $w_i$ are equal and the objective reduces to minimum Hamming weight. This optimization is the natural target of minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM). It is not, in general, degenerate quantum maximum-likelihood decoding, which sums probabilities over stabilizer-equivalent representatives.

# From a syndrome matrix to a detector graph

Assume each column of $H$ has weight at most two. Introduce a boundary vertex $b$ and construct a weighted multigraph $G=(V\cup\{b\},E)$:

- a weight-two column supported on checks $u$ and $v$ becomes an edge $(u,v)$;
- a weight-one column supported on $u$ becomes an edge $(u,b)$; and
- the edge receives the corresponding likelihood weight $w_i$.

Selecting an error vector is now equivalent to selecting an edge set $F\subseteq E$. The syndrome is its boundary: a detector vertex lies in $\partial F$ when it has odd degree in $F$. Let

$$
T=\{v\in V:s_v=1\}.
$$

If $|T|$ is odd, include the boundary vertex in the terminal set. The decoding problem is a minimum-weight $T$-join.

::: {#def-mwpm-t-join .callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition: $T$-join

For an even-cardinality set $T\subseteq V(G)$, a $T$-join is an edge set $F$ whose odd-degree vertices are exactly $T$:

$$
\partial F=T.
$$
:::

## Metric closure

For every pair $u,v\in T$, compute a shortest-path distance $d_G(u,v)$. Form the complete graph $K_T$ with edge weights $d_G$. A perfect matching of $K_T$ pairs all detection events; expanding each matched edge back to a shortest path in $G$ produces a $T$-join.

::: {#thm-mwpm-t-join-reduction .callout-important icon="false"}
## Theorem: reduction of minimum $T$-join to MWPM

If all relevant path weights are nonnegative and $|T|$ is even, the union of shortest paths associated with a minimum-weight perfect matching on the metric closure of $T$ is a minimum-weight $T$-join.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof

Take any $T$-join $F$. Each connected component of $(V,F)$ contains an even number of odd-degree vertices. By decomposing its edges into trails and cycles, pair the terminals using trails contained in $F$; cycles may be discarded when weights are nonnegative. Replacing each trail by a shortest path cannot increase the weight, so the optimal matching on the metric closure is no heavier than $F$.

Conversely, the symmetric difference of the shortest paths obtained from any perfect matching has odd boundary exactly at the matched terminals. It is therefore a $T$-join in the detector graph. The two inequalities prove equality of the optima.
:::

This reduction is the mathematical core of matching decoders for graph-like syndrome models. For surface-code noise with space-time syndrome extraction, vertices represent detection events in a three-dimensional decoding graph and edges represent elementary fault mechanisms [@dennis2002topological]. Correlated faults that create more than two detection events are hyperedges and do not fit this reduction without approximation or graph expansion.

# The perfect-matching polytope

Let $G=(V,E)$ now denote a graph with an even number of vertices, and let $x_e$ indicate whether edge $e$ belongs to a perfect matching. For $U\subseteq V$, let $\delta(U)$ be the cut consisting of edges with exactly one endpoint in $U$.

::: {#thm-mwpm-edmonds-polytope .callout-important icon="false"}
## Theorem: Edmonds' perfect-matching polytope

The convex hull of incidence vectors of perfect matchings is exactly the set of $x\in\mathbb{R}^E$ satisfying

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_e&\ge 0 &&(e\in E),\\
\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e&=1 &&(v\in V),\\
\sum_{e\in\delta(U)}x_e&\ge 1
&&(|U|\ge3\text{ odd}).
\end{aligned}
$$

The odd-set inequalities eliminate fractional solutions supported on odd cycles [@edmonds1965paths].
:::

The dual variables associated with tight odd sets organize into a laminar family. Algorithmically, a tight odd alternating cycle is contracted into a **blossom**. Search continues on the contracted graph; when an augmenting path is found, blossoms are expanded and the matching is lifted back to the original graph.

# Alternating paths and blossoms

::: {#def-mwpm-alternating-objects .callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition: alternating objects

Given a matching $M$:

- an alternating path alternates between edges outside and inside $M$;
- an augmenting path begins and ends at unmatched vertices; and
- a blossom is an odd alternating cycle together with a distinguished base vertex.
:::

Taking the symmetric difference of $M$ with an augmenting path increases $|M|$ by one. An odd alternating cycle obstructs the ordinary bipartite augmenting-path search because two even-level branches can meet. Blossom contraction preserves the existence of an augmenting path and allows the search to proceed. Weighted algorithms combine this combinatorial search with primal--dual updates that expose new tight edges. Modern implementations, such as Blossom V, refine the data structures and dual-update strategy while solving the same optimization problem [@kolmogorov2009blossom].

# Boundaries and repeated measurements

A surface-code patch has several boundary components, and a detection event may be paired either with another event or with a compatible boundary. One can represent this by explicit boundary vertices, duplicated boundary nodes in the metric closure, or a matching formulation that leaves designated boundary vertices unconstrained. The construction must ensure that boundary copies do not impose an artificial capacity-one constraint on a physical boundary.

With noisy measurement, matching is performed in a space-time graph. The decoder weight should be the negative log-likelihood of a path or fault mechanism, rather than its geometric length. Equal Manhattan weights are justified only for an idealized homogeneous noise model.

# What MWPM does and does not guarantee

MWPM returns a minimum-weight compatible chain for a graph-like model. It is polynomial-time and extremely effective for topological codes, but three qualifications matter:

1. It chooses a physical representative, not the most probable logical coset.
2. A weight-two detector graph omits higher-order correlations unless they are approximated.
3. A correction with the right boundary can still differ from the actual error by a logical cycle.

Tensor-network methods can approximately or exactly sum stabilizer-coset probabilities for some surface-code models [@bravyi2014efficient]. For general stabilizer codes, even optimal decoding is computationally hard [@iyer2015hardness], which motivates approximate decoders such as [belief propagation](belief-propagation.qmd) and [BP+OSD](bp-osd-decoding.qmd).
